buckets.label: Contract
buckets.hint: Binds you regardless of who runs the Board

buckets.label: Statute
buckets.hint: The Act, or the Supreme Court construing it

tasks.text: "Employees who act together about pay, hours, or working conditions are protected — whether or not there is a union."
tasks.reasoning: Section 7, and the words *concerted activity* do not contain the word *union*. This is the proposition most often assumed to have expired along with GC 23-02, and it is the one thing in this exercise that has not moved in decades.

tasks.text: "An employer must give notice and a genuine opportunity to bargain before changing wages, hours, or other terms and conditions of employment."
tasks.reasoning: Sections 8(a)(5) and 8(d). **The duty is statutory. The test for whether a contract clause waived it is not** — that is t6 and t4, and keeping the two apart is the whole point of this exercise. The duty does not weaken when the waiver standard loosens; only your defence does.

tasks.text: "A represented employee may request their union representative's presence at an investigatory interview they reasonably believe may result in discipline."
tasks.reasoning: *Weingarten* (1975) — the Supreme Court construing Section 7, which is why it sits at the statute layer rather than the doctrine layer. Compare t5, which is the Board's answer to a question *Weingarten* left open, and which has flipped twice.

tasks.text: "A management-rights clause reserving the right to 'implement changes in equipment' does not permit installing monitoring cameras on employees without bargaining."
tasks.reasoning: *Endurance Environmental Solutions* (373 NLRB No. 141, 10 December 2024) — decided on close to those facts, dash cameras in roughly 400 trucks. **It is the law today and it applies retroactively, and it was decided by a majority none of whom now sit.** Both halves of that sentence matter: do not discount it, and do not treat it as a fixed planning assumption.

tasks.text: "An unrepresented employee has no right to a co-worker's presence at an investigatory interview."
tasks.reasoning: *IBM Corp.*, 341 NLRB No. 148 (9 June 2004), withdrawing the right that *Epilepsy Foundation* had extended in 2000. **The same question, answered opposite ways, four years apart.** A later General Counsel urged reversal again; the Board did not, and the General Counsel left. This is what the doctrine layer looks like when you watch it for twenty years.

tasks.text: "Under the contract-coverage test, a change falling within the compass of a clause the parties negotiated may be made without further bargaining."
tasks.reasoning: *MV Transportation* (2019) — **and it is no longer good law**, having been overruled in 2024. The bucket still asks what kind of authority backs it, and the answer is Board doctrine. If you placed it in *Not established*, you read the question as *is this currently true*; the exercise asks *what kind of thing is this*, because that is what tells you how fast it can come back. Given the composition change of 7 August 2026, it can.

tasks.text: "Intrusive electronic monitoring and algorithmic management that tends to interfere with protected activity should be presumptively unlawful, and employers should be required to disclose it."
tasks.reasoning: GC 23-02, 31 October 2022 — **and note the word *should*.** It was never a holding. It was the agency's prosecuting arm announcing what it would urge the Board to find, and it was the most-cited document in this field for two years. It was rescinded on 14 February 2025 among 29 memoranda withdrawn at once.

tasks.text: "The agency's prosecuting arm is not currently advancing the theory that intrusive electronic monitoring interferes with Section 7 rights."
tasks.reasoning: **The rescission sits on the same layer as the memorandum.** A withdrawal is a General Counsel act, as fast and as reversible as the thing it withdrew. Which is why concluding from it that the exposure is gone is the layer error in its most expensive form: t1 did not move.

tasks.text: "The employer must give the union notice when AI implementation affects bargaining-unit work."
tasks.reasoning: CWA's provision at the Microsoft subsidiary ZeniMax, since reused as a template in tech. **True in the workplaces where it was negotiated, and not otherwise** — and notice is the most common AI provision in agreements generally. If you placed this at the statute layer you made the more forgivable error; if you placed it in *Not established* you may already owe it and not know.

tasks.text: "Sensor data may not be the sole basis for discipline, and a human must review context before AI-generated performance data is acted on."
tasks.reasoning: The UPS–Teamsters agreement. **Read it as a curriculum matter: this is the assist-versus-decide line and this track's rung boundary, written into a collective bargaining agreement by the other side of the table** — enforceable through grievance and arbitration rather than through a regulator. The craft you are learning is, in some workplaces, already a contractual obligation.

tasks.text: "Deploying AI that scores or disciplines bargaining-unit employees without bargaining is an unfair labor practice."
tasks.reasoning: **A strong inference from settled doctrine, and no Board decision holding it.** Every premise is solid — such a system touches terms and conditions, that makes it a mandatory subject, and after t4 your management-rights clause probably does not cover it. The conclusion is still an inference. Secondary sources state it as law; that is the sentence to stop trusting. *Unverifiable is not the same as false* — plan on it, and do not cite it.

tasks.text: "An employer must bargain before replacing bargaining-unit work with AI-generated output."
tasks.reasoning: SAG-AFTRA's charge against Llama Productions, filed May 2025 over an AI-generated voice performance, alleges exactly this. **A charge is not a holding**, and the Board has not opined on AI-driven displacement. Note that the practical answer does not wait for one: bargain it, or negotiate language that says what you may do.

pattern: The expensive direction is treating something as more settled than it is — a prosecutorial theory read as a right, an inference read as a holding, a negotiated term read as the law. The cheap-looking direction costs too: assuming a statute stopped applying because a memorandum was withdrawn.
postscript: Check **t8 against t1** first. If you placed t8 anywhere and concluded the exposure went with it, you have made this module's central error — a General Counsel withdrew a theory and Section 7 did not move. Then **t2 against t4 and t6**: the *duty* to bargain is statutory and the *test for whether your clause waived it* is doctrine, and the second is what flipped in 2019 and again in 2024. Practitioners who conflate them believe the duty itself loosened. Then **t9 and t10** — if you put either at the statute layer, you are describing an obligation you may not owe; if you put either in *Not established*, you may owe it by contract already and be discovering it in a grievance. And **t11** last, because it is the proposition most likely to arrive in a briefing this year stated as settled law. It is a good inference. It is not a holding, and the difference shows up the moment somebody asks you to cite it.
